system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.

   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the

### Contract 767FSupp2d1191_confidential_memorandum_for_the

#### c019 — Redemption payment and suspension

```
Payment for redeerned Shares will be made in cash within seven days after the redemption date; provided, however, that Wells Fargo reserves the right to postpone payment of the redemption price (without liability for interest or income thereon) or to suspend redemption rights in certain circumstances as specified In the Declaration of Trust.
```

- **d01** (risk type 2.2, scope `case` — needs 767FSupp2d1191_october_24_2000_declaration): The CI Term Trust Memorandum’s statement that payment for redeemed shares “will be made in cash” conflicted with the Declaration’s discretion to redeem shares in cash or securities.
  Opinion lines 86-87:
```
With respect to Plaintiffs exit from the Trust and the Program. Plaintiff contends that Wells Fargo breached the agreements by refusing to return the loaned securities unless Plaintiff paid the collateral shortfall, by failing to redeem the Trust shares for cash, and by requiring Plaintiff to accept a segregated account holding the collateral investments during the wind down. Wells Fargo argues that actions were either expressly permitted by the contracts or were within Wells Fargo’s broad discretion to manage the Trust.
I will not grant summary judgment to Wells Fargo on the contract claims concerning Plaintiffs attempts to exit the Program. Again, there are ambiguities in the relevant documents. While the SLA provides that Plaintiff assumes the risk of collateral deficiencies, it also provides that Wells Fargo will be responsible for returning the collateral to the borrowers, which could arguably create an ambiguity about whether the shortfall had to be made up before or after the loaned securities were returned. Similarly, with respect to redemption of Trust shares, Section 5.2 of the Declaration gave the Trustee discretion to redeem Trust shares in cash or securities, whereas the Confidential Memoranda for the two Funds provide that redemption would be in cash. Again, resolving the conflict between these terms is an issue of fact and so summary judgment is not appropriate. Finally, disaggregating the collateral investments into pro rata accounts in which some portions were too small to be sold may violate the contractual requirements of liquidity in the investments.
```

#### c020 — Limitations of Liability

```
Limitations of Liability and Indemnification Wells Fargo and other agents of the Trust shall have no liability to the Trust or the Shareholders for any act or omission, provided that such act or omission does not involve bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard of its duties to the Trust.
```

- **d02** (risk type 2.2, scope `case` — needs 767FSupp2d1191_october_24_2000_declaration): The CI Term Trust Memorandum’s exception to immunity for ordinary “negligence” conflicted with the Declaration’s gross-negligence standard, leaving unresolved which liability threshold governed the transaction as a whole.
  Opinion lines 78-79:
```
I next turn to the meaning and effect of Section 8.1. I agree with Plaintiff that Section 8.1 cannot be viewed in isolation, since the Securities Lending Program and the investment of Plaintiffs collateral were governed by numerous other documents, including the SLA, the Subscription Agreement, and the Confidential Memoranda, not just the Declaration. Knut. Co. v. Knutson Constr. Co., 433 N.W.2d 149, 151 (Minn.App.1988) (“A contract and several writings relating to the same transaction must be construed with reference to each other.”). The other documents provide a lesser standard for liability. Under the SLA, Wells Fargo “assumes the risk of loss arising from negligent and fraudulent operation of its Securities Lending Program.” SLA, ¶ 8 (emphasis added) (also providing that Plaintiff assumes the risks of “collateral deficiencies or collateral investment loss”). Similarly, in other documents, Wells Fargo assumed responsibility for negligent conduct. See Confidential Memorandum for the EY Series, Exh. A-4 to Def.’s Mot. for Summ J., ECF No. 294-4 (“Wells Fargo ... shall have no liability to the Trust or the Shareholders for any act or omission, provided that such act or omission does not involve bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard of its duties to the Trustee”) (emphasis added).
Considering the documents together, I conclude there is an ambiguity in the conflict between the “gross negligence” standard of the Declaration and the simple negligence standard of the SLA and other documents. Resolution of the interplay among these various provisions, and whether any should be given primacy, should be done by a fact-finder. In addition, I note that the Declaration’s limitation of liability applies first to “any act performed or omitted by such Covered Person in good faith on behalf of the Trust ... and in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority conferred on such Covered Person by this Declaration.” There is at a minimum a factual question as to whether that description would include the alleged negligent investment of the collateral in risky securities when such conduct is expressly in conflict with the investment objective set forth in the SLA; there is nothing in the Declaration to indicate that covered persons had the authority to violate their own investment standards. Moreover, the second provision of the limitation (providing that a covered person “shall be liable for any loss, damage or claim incurred by reason of such Covered Person’s bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard of the duties involved in the conduct of his or her office”) could be read as a non-exclusive, rather than exclusive, description, of the type of conduct that will give rise to liability. In that case, there would be no conflict with the negligence standards set forth in the other documents.
```

- **d12** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): Section 8.4’s references to a Covered Person’s “good faith reliance” and replacement of duties were unclear as to whether they eliminated all noncontractual duties, as Wells Fargo argued, or applied only when the person relied on a specific Declaration provision that conflicted with a common-law duty.
  Opinion lines 70-77:
```
Wells Fargo argues that, despite the existence of numerous documents and contracts governing the parties’ relationship, the provisions in the Declaration of Trust are paramount and limit its liability. It points to two provisions in the Declaration that it claims relieve it of liability for all but certain claims and types of conduct, specifically Sections 8.1 and 8.4.
Section 8.4 provides:
To the extent that, at law or equity, a Covered Person has duties (including fiduciary duties) and liabilities relating to the Trust or any Series thereof or to any Shareholder, any such Covered Person acting under this Declaration shall not be liable to the Trust or any Series thereof or to any Shareholder for the Covered Person’s good faith reliance on the provisions of this Declaration. The provisions of this Declaration, to the extent that they restrict or limit the duties and liabilities of a Covered Person otherwise existing at law or in equity, are agreed by the parties hereto to replace such other duties and liabilities of such Covered Person.
Declaration, Exh. A-1 to Def.’s Mot. for Summ J., ECF No. 294-1. Wells Fargo argues that this means Plaintiffs non-contract claims are barred.
Section 8.1, set forth in full above, provides that the Trustee and others shall not be liable “by reason of any act performed or omitted by such Covered Person in good faith on behalf of the Trust ... and in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority conferred on such Covered Person by this Declaration” except that a covered person may be liable for losses or damages caused by that person’s “bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or reckless disregard of the duties involved in the conduct of his or her office.” Declaration, Exh. A-l to Def.’s Mot. for Summ J., ECF No. 294-1. The Declaration contains a similar limitation for “errors of judgment or mistakes of fact or law.” Id., Sec. 9.2. Wells Fargo argues that this means the it can only be liable for conduct that amounts to bad faith or gross negligence, and that Plaintiff cannot prove that Wells Fargo engaged in any conduct meeting that threshold.
In response, however, Plaintiff points out that there are other agreements relevant to the parties’ relationship that contain different standards for the Trustee’s conduct. Plaintiff further argues that ambiguity in the Declaration’s provisions means that the interpretation of these clauses, alone or in combination with the ofher agreements, is an issue of fact for the jury and not appropriate for summary judgment. I agree with Plaintiff.
“[T]he primary goal of contract interpretation is to determine and enforce the intent of the parties.” Motorsports Racing Plus, Inc. v. Arctic Cat Sales, Inc., 666 N.W.2d 320, 323 (Minn.2003). “When interpreting a contract, we must determine if the language is clear and unambiguous, meaning it has only one reasonable interpretation.” Halla Nursery, Inc. v. City of Chanhassen, 781 N.W.2d 880, 884 (Minn. 2010) (citation omitted). In determining whether there is ambiguity I examine the meaning of the words and phrases in accordance with the apparent purpose of the contract as a whole. Id. If the contract is unambiguous, I must give effect to the language of the contract. Id. I must construe a contract in such a manner as to give effect to all its terms and in the context of the full agreement. Metropolitan Airports Comm’n v. Noble, 763 N.W.2d 639, 645 (Minn.2009); Porch v. Gen. Motors Acceptance Corp., 642 N.W.2d 473, 477 (Minn.App.2002). Determination of whether a contract is ambiguous and, if unambiguous, determination of its meaning, are legal questions. 301 Clifton Place L.L.C. v. 301 Clifton Place Condo. Ass’n, 783 N.W.2d 551, 564 (Minn.App. 2010). However, if I conclude the agreement or any term is ambiguous, its meaning is a question of fact for the jury or other fact-fínder. Id. at 565.
I first examine the effect of Section 8.4. I agree with Plaintiff that this provision does not unambiguously eliminate all non-contractual duties. Rather, it replaces common law duties with contractual duties where two circumstances apply: (1) the covered person has relied in good faith on a specific provision of the Declaration in taking some action and (2) that provision conflicts with a common law duty. As noted by Plaintiff, Wells Fargo does not identify any specific provision it purports to have acted in compliance with in good faith or how that provision conflicts with a common law duty. Accordingly, Wells Fargo is not entitled to summary judgment on the non-contract claims on the basis of Section 8.4 of the Declaration.
```
